setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}, where staff are starting to try new technology tools.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you are among the first to try new technology tools your team is considering.
detail: A tool demo was shown at last week's meeting.
pressure: {coworker3} says everyone else is already using these tools.
You are behind on a deadline.

tiers.1: Protecting private information comes before trying anything new.
tiers.2: A new tool needs approval before real work goes into it.
tiers.3: Check what a new tool produces before relying on it.
tiers.4: Ask for training before using an unfamiliar feature on live work.
tiers.5: Sharing a good idea about a tool can wait behind urgent problems.

fact: {coworker} wants to paste customer details into a new online tool, and the policy says customer details stay in approved systems.
issues.short: the customer details going into the new tool
issues.action: Keep the customer details out of the tool and tell {lead|the} you want it reviewed.
issues.brief: keep the details out and ask for a review
issues.reason: Details pasted into an unapproved tool leave the workplace's control and cannot be taken back.
issues.lesson: Keep private information in approved systems, however useful a new tool looks.

shortcut.text: Paste only a few of the details, since a small amount is not much risk.
shortcut.why: Even a few customer details leave approved systems, which the policy does not allow.
shortcut.mis: A small amount of private data is harmless.

clear: {Lead|the} already told {coworker} to keep customer details out of a new online tool.
issues.done: the customer details are already protected

fact: You found a scheduling app online that could save time, and the policy says new tools need approval before real work goes in.
issues.action: Ask {lead|the} to approve the app before any real work goes into it.
issues.brief: ask for approval before using it
issues.reason: Approval lets someone check security and cost before the team depends on a tool.
issues.lesson: Get a new tool approved before putting real work into it.

shortcut.text: Try it with this week's real schedule to see whether it is worth asking about.
shortcut.brief: test it on the real schedule
shortcut.why: Real work in an unapproved tool breaks the policy and can be hard to move out.
shortcut.mis: You need to try a tool before you can ask about it.

clear: {Lead|the} already approved a scheduling app for use at work.

fact: A new tool summarized a report for you, but the summary's totals do not match the totals in the report's table.
issues.short: the summary that does not match the report
issues.action: Compare the summary with the report and correct the totals before using it.
issues.brief: check the summary against the report
issues.reason: New tools can produce confident mistakes. Checking against the source is how you find them.
issues.lesson: Check a new tool's output against the source before relying on it.

shortcut.text: Use the summary as it is, since a new tool is probably more accurate than people.
shortcut.brief: use the summary as it is
shortcut.why: The totals disagree, so at least one is wrong. Only the source can settle it.
shortcut.mis: New technology is more accurate than people.

clear: You already compared a tool-written summary with its report and fixed the totals.

fact: The new system has a feature you are not trained on, and the guide says untrained staff should not use it on live records.
issues.short: the feature you have not been trained on
issues.action: Ask {lead|the} for training before using the feature on live records.
issues.reason: Untrained use on live records can change things that are hard to undo.
issues.lesson: Ask for training before using an unfamiliar feature on live records.

shortcut.text: Learn it on live records and undo anything that goes wrong.
shortcut.why: Some changes cannot be undone, and the guide does not allow untrained use on live records.
shortcut.mis: Mistakes on live records are easy to reverse.

clear: You already finished training for a new system feature.

fact: You think a new tool could help the whole team, and {lead|the} says new tools are tried first with one small group.
issues.short: your idea to use the tool across the team
issues.action: Suggest a small trial with one group, as {lead|the} described.
issues.reason: A small trial shows what works before everyone depends on the tool.
issues.lesson: Try a new tool with a small group before rolling it out.

shortcut.text: Set it up for the whole team tonight so everyone benefits right away.
shortcut.brief: roll it out to everyone tonight
shortcut.why: Skipping the trial means problems reach everyone at once.

proceed.text: Carry on with your regular work, since nothing here needs action.
proceed.why: Each of these situations involves a new tool that needs a response from you.
proceed.lesson: New technology still follows the workplace's rules for data, approval and checking.

generic.text: Ask {coworker2} how they use the tool and do the same.
generic.why: A coworker's habit is not the policy, and they may be using it unsafely.
generic.mis: If others use a tool, it must be allowed.

generic.text: Wait until the tool causes a problem, then ask {lead|the} about it.
generic.why: Waiting means the problem can happen before anyone has checked the tool.
generic.mis: Questions can wait until something goes wrong.

overcaution.text: Refuse to use any new tool until {lead|the} approves every one on the market.
overcaution.why: The concern is one specific tool. Refusing all of them blocks approved work.
overcaution.mis: Every new tool is off limits.

setup: {Lead|the} asks you to find out whether a new tool could help your team.

steps.text: Name the problem the tool should solve
Try it with one small group
Check the results against current work

rel: The request should explain what the tool is for.
You can only check results after trying it.
process.lesson: Name the need, get approval, try it small, then check the results.

title: Trying new tools
intro: You are reviewing a draft guide for staff who want to try new tools.
doc.lesson: A guide to new tools must protect private data, require approval and check results.

lines.text: Keep customer details out of tools that are not approved.

bad.text: Test a new tool with real customer details to see how well it works.
bad.why: Real customer details should stay in approved systems, even for a test.

lines.text: Ask for approval before putting real work into a new tool.
lines.fine: Lets the workplace check the tool first.

bad.text: Start using a new tool and ask for approval if it works well.
bad.why: Approval comes before real work goes in, not after the tool proves itself.

lines.text: Check what a new tool produces against the original source.

bad.text: Trust a new tool's results once it has been right a few times.
bad.why: A few correct results do not show it will be right next time. Check each time that it matters.

lines.text: Try a new tool with one small group before the whole team.
lines.fine: Limits the effect of any problems.

review.notes: Rules are stated as this workplace's policy. No product, vendor or law is named. Tiers: private data, approval, checking output, training, trial.
